progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c14 (addition polymerisation; the two C=C carbons form the backbone and everything else hangs off; drawing a repeat unit with brackets, n and continuation bonds; recovering the monomer by restoring the C=C, adding no H; dispersion contact; thermoplastics); chem-m7-c15 (two reactive ends; ester and amide links; the repeat unit as one of each monomer minus the water; "add the water back"; count the C=O carbons; addition against condensation; nylon's hydrogen bonds; melting does not break chain links); chem-m7-c10 (ester naming, for "methyl 2-methylpropenoate", screen only); chem-m7-c05 (hydrogen bonding needs H on N or O); chem-m7-c08b (dipole–dipole from C=O); chem-m7-c01 (locants).
progression.startsWith: Draw the repeating unit from a monomer. The video opens: Polymer questions usually come in four shapes.
progression.stopsAfter: four worked HSC-style questions and a decision board: find the backbone first.

teaching.task: Can you draw a polymer from its monomer, find the monomers from a polymer, decide whether it formed by addition or condensation, and explain one of its properties from its structure?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why only two carbons join the backbone: only the C=C opens (2b, 2d). Why three units give three ethyl groups and six backbone carbons: one side group and two backbone carbons per unit (2c). Why Q2's polymer is condensation: its backbone contains ester links (3b). Why every link gets water: each was made by losing one (3c, 3d). Why each monomer must have two reactive ends: each must link twice (3c, 4c). Why X is addition despite its ester group: the backbone is C–C; the ester is a side group (4b, 4d). Why no H is added to X's monomer: restoring the C=C completes each carbon's four bonds (4b; c14). Why one monomer can make Y: it carries both reactive groups (4c). Why nylon melts far higher than P: same skeleton, but N–H allows hydrogen bonds between chains (5b, 5c). Why melting does not depend on link strength: melting separates chains (5d).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Polymer questions come in four shapes (draw a chain from a monomer, find the monomers from a chain, decide addition or condensation, and explain a property), and each starts with the same move: find the backbone, the line of atoms that runs through the brackets. Q1 (but-1-ene for hot-water pipes) opens only the double bond, so carbon one becomes CH2 and carbon two a CH carrying the ethyl group, then joins three units head to tail and circles one; the classic mistake puts all four carbons in the chain. Q2 (a carpet-fibre section) traces a backbone through oxygens and C=O groups, names the ester links and the repeat unit, and adds the water back at every link to recover propane-1,3-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid; the mistake cuts only one link. Q3 (polymers X and Y) looks along each backbone: X has an ester group only as a side group on a carbon chain, so it is an addition polymer whose monomer puts the double bond back, while Y has ester links in the chain and the stated water release, so it is a condensation polymer of lactic acid; the mistake calls X a polyester. Q4 lines up nylon 6,6 and polyester P on the same skeleton, finds the one difference, the N-H, and explains that hydrogen bonds between nylon chains take more energy to overcome; the mistake says the links break on melting. A decision board gathers the moves.
teaching.openingDecision: Polymer questions usually come in four shapes. Draw a chain from a monomer. Find the monomers from a chain. Decide whether it formed by addition or condensation. And explain a property. Each one starts with the same move: find the backbone, the line of atoms that runs through the brackets. Here are four HSC-style questions. Pause and try each one, then we'll work it through, one step at a time.
teaching.understandingCheck: Four, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a, 5a): the monomer's name and formula and the "three repeat units" and "circle" demands (Q1); the full two-unit section and both demands (Q2); both repeat units and both demands (Q3); both repeat units, both melting points and the "with reference to their structures" demand (Q4). Nothing answer-bearing during the holds; the backbone strip dims.
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017, p56), as printed: "model and compare the structure, properties and uses of addition polymers of ethylene and related monomers, for example: - polyethylene (PE) - polyvinyl chloride (PVC) - polystyrene (PS) - polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) (ACSCH136)" "model and compare the structure, properties and uses of condensation polymers, for example: - nylon - polyesters" Practice and transfer only. The coverage rows stay with chem-m7-c14 (C7-IQ6-01) and chem-m7-c15 (C7-IQ6-02); G04 adds a practice row, not first coverage. starts at the route's "Draw the repeating unit from a monomer" and stops at its "Classify addition or condensation and explain one property from structure". Four questions, one per route skill, each with a trap: draw a three-unit section of an addition polymer from but-1-ene (putting all four carbons in the backbone); recover the monomers from a section of a polyester (cutting only one of the links); classify two polymers as addition or condensation and draw each monomer (calling a polymer with an ester side group a polyester); explain why a polyamide melts far above a polyester with the same carbon skeleton (saying melting breaks the stronger amide bonds). One move links all four: find the backbone, the line of atoms that runs through the brackets. Not here: new teaching of addition or condensation polymerisation (c14 and c15; recalled in one clause each); PE, PVC, PS and PTFE property questions (c14's attempts; the decision board recalls them in one line); hydrolysis questions (c15 scene 7; not examined here); copolymers of two alkenes (beyond the site lessons; author note a); the acid chloride route; natural polymers, Kevlar, thermosets, recycling and lifecycle (route review change 4 and site L23's own "extension" label); mechanisms and conditions.

design.visualSystem: As g01: the question card at the top (shrinking to a strip during the walkthrough), a type badge at its left ("Draw from a monomer", "Find the monomers", "Addition or condensation?", "Property from structure"), the structure board or chain view at the centre, answer boxes at the right, and a three-row backbone strip at the far left (this video's check strip): "Find the backbone (through the brackets)", "All C–C: addition. Open or close the C=C.", "Ester or amide links: condensation. Remove or add the water." Rows tick as each question uses them.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on and four stimulus thumbnails fan out on the right, one per question shape; each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card writes with its structure and any context plate small at its corner; the walkthrough shrinks the card to a strip, lights the type badge and underlines each given as it is used; a locant counter numbers the monomer's carbons as its C=C pulses; the section builder slides three opened monomers together and a ring circles one repeat unit; the backbone tracer runs along each section or repeat unit and colours the links it passes; c10's cut line drops through each ester link as the water insert docks OH and H; the X and Y structures enlarge in turn and the kept one dims to a chip; the two repeat units align and their matching segments light in pairs; c14's chain view splits into nylon and polyester boxes with dotted hydrogen bonds drawn only on the nylon side; each question ends with its classic mistake chip taking a grey scribble cross; the backbone strip returns as a two-column board, each row lighting on its cue with its question badge; scene crossfade with settle.
